Where is Indianapolis and how is it laid out?

Indianapolis is the capital of Indiana and the county seat of Marion County, sitting on the West Fork of the White River in the middle of the state. It is about 107 miles north of Louisville and 164 miles southeast of Chicago.

The city is a consolidated city-county. Its limits match Marion County except for four separate towns and cities: Beech Grove, Lawrence, Southport and Speedway. Nine civil townships divide the county: Center, Decatur, Franklin, Lawrence, Perry, Pike, Warren, Washington and Wayne. When a seller says the house is in Perry Township or Pike Township, that is a real map location with its own schools, fire and assessor boundaries.

The city covers 367.94 square miles, with 361.64 of that as land. Unigov, the 1970 consolidation, took effect on January 1, 1970 and added more than 300 square miles and about 250,000 people. A house in the old mile-square core and a house in a later township subdivision can have very different ages, lot sizes and utility setups.

How did Indianapolis grow, and what does that mean for older houses?

Indianapolis was a planned city, laid out in 1821 by Alexander Ralston and Elias Pym Fordham as a one-mile-square grid around a central circle. State government moved from Corydon at the start of 1825, and the National Road opened through town in 1827.

Housing followed the transit lines. The city's streetcar suburbs include Broad Ripple, Irvington and University Heights, and Indianapolis has 13 local historic districts and five conservation areas. Examples listed for the districts include Chatham-Arch, Fountain Square, Lockerbie Square, Old Northside, Irvington and Woodruff Place.

For a seller, age shows up in the details a buyer prices in:

  • Original knob-and-tube wiring or older panels in pre-war homes.
  • Clay or cast iron sewer laterals under mature trees.
  • Brick foundations, wet basements and old plaster.
  • Exterior changes in a historic district that may need review before work starts.

The city counts 99 statistical neighborhood areas and roughly 500 registered neighborhood associations, so an HOA or association may also have its own rules about exterior work or signs.

The Census Bureau's QuickFacts for Indianapolis shows a median owner-occupied home value of $224,800 for 2020 to 2024 and an owner-occupied rate of 56.0%. That means nearly half of households rent, which matters if your house has tenants.

What drives the Indianapolis economy?

Indianapolis has a broad economy anchored by life sciences, logistics, health insurance and manufacturing. Three Fortune 500 companies are headquartered here: Elevance Health, Eli Lilly and Corteva.

Eli Lilly is the largest private employer, with about 11,000 workers. Amazon is listed at about 9,000, FedEx at about 7,000 across 35 facilities, Rolls-Royce North America at about 4,000 and Allison Transmission at about 2,500. The airport is the site of FedEx Express's National Hub, and the metro area's life sciences cluster has nearly 350 companies.

Tourism adds to the mix, with 29.2 million visitors a year reported. Job changes at large employers can affect nearby housing demand, and an owner facing a relocation or transfer may want a sale on a set date.

What weather and flood risks affect an Indianapolis house?

Indianapolis has a humid continental climate with hot summers, cold winters and rain in every month. July averages 75.4 degrees and January averages 28.1 degrees, with 42.4 inches of rain and 25.9 inches of snow in a typical year. May is the wettest month, at 5.05 inches on average.

The record high is 106 degrees and the record low is minus 27. That swing is hard on roofs, gutters, driveways and HVAC equipment.

The White River runs 31 miles through the city and is fed by about 35 streams, including Eagle Creek, Fall Creek, Pleasant Run and Pogue's Run. Homes near those waterways may sit in mapped flood zones, and a lender may require flood insurance. You can check a parcel on FEMA's flood map service before you list.

  • Check the gutters and grading if a basement has ever taken water.
  • Keep receipts for roof or drainage work, since buyers ask.
  • Photograph any storm damage before repairs.

How do roads and transit affect where Indianapolis sellers are?

Indianapolis is ringed by I-465, a 53-mile beltway completed on October 5, 1970, and crossed by I-65, I-70, I-69 and I-74. The I-65 and I-70 inner loop includes the North Split, which carries more than 200,000 vehicles a day, and a $350 million reconstruction began in 2021.

IndyGo runs the Red Line, a 13.1-mile bus rapid transit route that began service on September 1, 2019 between Broad Ripple Village and the University of Indianapolis. The 15.2-mile Purple Line opened in October 2024 and links downtown to Lawrence. A 24-mile Blue Line from Cumberland to the airport broke ground on February 28, 2025, with opening expected in 2028.

Indianapolis International Airport opened its current terminal on November 11, 2008. Sellers near a new rapid transit corridor or a long highway project often find that buyers ask about it, so be ready to say how close the house is and what you know about timing.

What city rules should an Indianapolis seller know about?

The city requires owners of residential rental units to register them, and the Department of Business and Neighborhood Services (DBNS) runs the registry. If you are selling a rented house, a tenant's lease, the registry record and any open code issues all become part of the sale conversation.

Short-term rentals have their own rules. A permit program took effect on January 1, 2025, with a one-time $150 fee for the first permit and no fee for renewals. The ordinance also requires short-term rentals to be in a legally built dwelling that meets applicable building code. DBNS is at 200 E Washington St, and its phone is 317-327-8700.

Vacant houses face a newer tool. News reports on the city's Continuous Vacancy program say it started January 1, 2026 and targets homes that have gone six years without improvement. Repair orders can last up to two years, and negligent owners can be fined up to $5,000 per year, with fines adjusted if the owner works with DBNS. The same reports say about 60% of eligible properties are held by out-of-state owners. If you inherited a vacant Indianapolis house, check with DBNS before the problem grows.

How does a sale close and get recorded in Marion County?

In Marion County, a deed must be stamped by the Assessor's Office in Room W121 of the City-County Building before the Recorder will record it. The Recorder's Office is in Suite T-741 at 200 E. Washington Street.

The recorder says it will stop providing forms or documents for recording as of September 29, 2026, so the deed needs to come from your title company, attorney or another preparer. Documents can be submitted by mail, through e-recording partners or in person. The office phone is 317-327-4020.

Indiana also uses a sales disclosure form. Under IC 6-1.1-5.5-3, the parties to the transfer complete it, the county assessor reviews it, and it is filed with the county auditor before the conveyance document is filed. Property tax bills in Indiana are due in two installments, May 10 and November 10, and the state homestead deduction is the lesser of $45,000 or 60% of gross assessed value. Your closing agent will prorate those amounts.

  • Ask for a payoff letter if any mortgage or lien is on the house.
  • Gather landlord registry details if the house is rented.
  • Confirm any open code orders with DBNS.

What do Indianapolis sellers usually face?

Most Indianapolis sellers who want speed are dealing with one of a short list of problems. Which one it is changes how fast a sale can go.

  • An inherited house that needs probate, clean-out or repairs.
  • A rental with a tenant, deferred maintenance or a registry question.
  • A vacant house that has drawn code attention.
  • An older home with plumbing, electrical or foundation issues.
  • A move for work that leaves a mortgage and an empty house.

A cash purchase can skip lender appraisals and repair requests, but you should still compare it with a normal listing. Ask any buyer for the offer in writing, confirm who is paying for title and recording, and read the contract before you sign.

Do I have to register a rental house in Indianapolis before selling?

Owners of residential rental units in Indianapolis are required to register them with the city. If the house is currently rented, make sure the registry record is current so the sale paperwork lines up.

How long does recording a deed take in Marion County?

The Recorder's Office does not publish a fixed turnaround on its main page. The deed must first be stamped by the Assessor's Office in Room W121, then submitted by mail, e-recording or in person. Your title company can tell you the timing for your closing.

Does Indianapolis have a short-term rental permit?

Yes. A short-term rental permit program began January 1, 2025, with a one-time $150 fee for the first permit and no renewal fee. The unit must be a legally built dwelling that meets applicable building code.

What is the Continuous Vacancy program?

News reports describe it as a DBNS enforcement program starting January 1, 2026 for vacant homes that have gone six years without improvement. Repair orders can run up to two years, and fines can reach $5,000 per year.

When are Indiana property taxes due?

Indiana property tax is due in two installments, May 10 and November 10. Your closing agent usually prorates the current installment between buyer and seller.

Can I sell an Indianapolis house that needs major repairs?

Yes. You can sell it as is, though a lender-financed buyer may require repairs or an inspection fix. A cash buyer can buy without those requirements, so compare the written terms before choosing.

Where is Fort Wayne, Indiana, and what shapes its layout?

Fort Wayne is the Allen County seat, in northeastern Indiana, 18 miles west of the Ohio border and 50 miles south of Michigan. Three rivers meet here: the St. Joseph, the St. Marys and the Maumee, which flows on to Lake Erie.

Residents describe the city in four unofficial quadrants. Calhoun Street separates southwest from southeast, and the rivers mark the other divisions. Named historic districts include Williams-Woodland Park and Forest Park Boulevard. Elevation is about 758 feet.

Where your house sits among those quadrants and rivers will affect flood questions, school boundaries and how long a drive to work is, so it is worth stating plainly in any conversation with a buyer.

What is the short history of Fort Wayne?

Fort Wayne grew at a river portage. The Miami people built Kekionga at the confluence, and the U.S. Army built Fort Wayne in 1794 under Anthony Wayne after the Battle of Fallen Timbers.

The city was platted in 1823, incorporated as a town in 1829 and as a city on February 22, 1840. The Wabash and Erie Canal and later the railroads drove growth, and the "Summit City" nickname comes from the canal's high point.

How serious is flooding in Fort Wayne?

Flooding is the biggest weather story in the city's history. The Great Flood of 1913 killed seven people, left about 15,000 homeless and damaged more than 5,500 buildings. In 1982, a second flood forced 9,000 residents to evacuate and damaged 2,000 buildings, with losses of $56.1 million in 1982 dollars.

A $50 million flood control project followed, and it included Headwaters Park. The climate otherwise is humid continental, with about 38 to 39 inches of precipitation and about 33.5 inches of snow a year. The city averages roughly 39 thunderstorm days annually, and its record high is 106 degrees Fahrenheit (June 28, 2012) against a record low of minus 24 (January 12, 1918).

For a seller, the practical step is to check the property's flood zone and any insurance requirement before you list. A buyer's lender will do so anyway, and surprises there can delay a closing.

Four public districts serve the city. Your mailing address does not always tell you which one applies, so confirm it on the district's boundary tool before you describe schools to a buyer.

  • East Allen County Schools.
  • Northwest Allen County Schools.
  • Southwest Allen County Schools.

Interstate 69 is the only Interstate through the city, and I-469 is the beltway. U.S. Routes 24, 27, 30 and 33 cross the city, as do State Roads 1, 3, 14, 37 and 930. Fort Wayne International Airport handles commercial flights, and Smith Field handles general aviation. About 85 percent of residents commute alone by car, and the nearest Amtrak stop is Waterloo Station, about 25 miles north.

Higher education in the city includes Indiana University Fort Wayne and Purdue University Fort Wayne (both established in 2018), Ivy Tech, Indiana Tech, the University of Saint Francis and Concordia Theological Seminary.

How does Fort Wayne enforce housing and vacant-property rules?

The city's Neighborhood Code Compliance office, part of Community Development, enforces minimum housing standards. It works on unsafe structures, secures vacant ones and cleans up blighted areas. Its list of issues also covers tall grass and weeds, abandoned or inoperable vehicles, and a protocol for meth-related properties.

  • Phone: 311 or 260-427-1127.
  • Office: 200 E. Berry St., Suite 320, Fort Wayne, IN 46802.
  • Forms: the office publishes a Housing Registration Form, instructions and the residential code online.

Under Chapter 152 of the city code, inspectors may enter with probable cause or the owner's consent, and they can seek a warrant under Indiana Code 36-7-9-16 if access is refused. A premises that is unsealed, unsecured and vacant can be declared a public nuisance and gets a full inspection.

A city update from Community Development, undated, reported 259 demolitions since 2015 under the statewide Blight Elimination Program and 44 more planned for that year. The money came from the U.S. Treasury through the Indiana Housing and Community Development Authority. If your house has an open order to repair or demolish, say so at the start. It changes the price and the path to closing, but it does not rule out a sale.

A sale in Allen County needs a Sales Disclosure Form signed by both parties, reviewed by the county assessor and filed with the county auditor. Under Indiana Code 6-1.1-5.5 the auditor cannot accept the deed without it. A $20 fee applies, except for transfers such as foreclosure, divorce, probate or condemnation.

Property tax is billed in two installments. The Department of Local Government Finance lists May 11 and November 10 for 2026, with a 5 percent penalty for a payment within 30 days of the due date and 10 percent after that. In a 2024 report, the Allen County Treasurer's office described its location as the Rousseau Centre, 1 E. Main St., Suite 104, and its mailing address as PO Box 2540, Fort Wayne, IN 46801. Its phone number in that report was 260-449-7693. Check the county site for current details.

Ask the county for a statement of what is owed on the parcel before you set a closing date, so the figure on your settlement sheet is no surprise.

What are my options for selling a house in Fort Wayne?

You can list with an agent, sell it yourself or take a cash offer, and the choice turns on condition, timing and whether anyone is living in the home.

  • A listing makes sense if the home shows well and you can wait for a buyer's financing and inspection.
  • A private sale saves a listing fee but puts the paperwork and negotiation on you.
  • A cash offer fits houses that need repairs, inherited homes and sellers with a firm deadline.

Yes. Neighborhood Code Compliance, within Community Development, secures vacant structures and handles unsafe buildings. You can reach it at 311 or 260-427-1127.

Yes, for most sales with consideration. Both parties sign it, the assessor reviews it and the county auditor needs it before accepting the deed. The fee is $20 with some exceptions.

It can be. The city had major floods in 1913 and 1982, and a flood control project followed. Check the property's flood zone before listing so a lender's questions do not surprise you.

Where is Evansville, Indiana, and how big is it?

Evansville is the seat of Vanderburgh County in southwestern Indiana, on a bend of the Ohio River. It is the third-largest city in the state after Indianapolis and Fort Wayne, and it covers about 47.9 square miles.

Most of the city sits in a shallow valley ringed by low hills, with the west side on higher ground. The 38th parallel crosses the north side of town. Downtown grew from an original plat of about 200 acres and still holds early twentieth-century buildings.

What is the history of Evansville?

Hugh McGary Jr. bought about 441 acres in 1812 and called the site McGary's Landing. It was renamed Evansville in 1814 for Colonel Robert Morgan Evans, incorporated in 1817 and chartered as a city in 1847.

The Wabash and Erie Canal and early railroads boosted trade, and hardwood furniture made Evansville a manufacturing center, with 41 factories by 1900. The Graham Brothers built trucks here from 1916 to 1929. In World War II the city produced 167 LSTs, the nation's largest inland output, and 6,242 P-47 fighters. The National Park Service designated Evansville Indiana's American World War II Heritage City on December 6, 2022.

Thirteen neighborhoods are listed as National Register historic districts, and the Riverside district is known for tree-lined brick streets and turn-of-the-century homes. Who are the major employers around Evansville?

Health care, manufacturing and finance headline the list of Evansville employers. Berry Global and OneMain Financial are headquartered here, and Escalade, Old National Bank and Shoe Carnival are NASDAQ-listed companies based in the city.

  • Health care: Deaconess Health System and Ascension St. Vincent.
  • Manufacturing and pharma: Mead Johnson and Bristol-Myers Squibb.
  • Nearby plants: Alcoa in Newburgh, SABIC in Mount Vernon and Toyota in Princeton.
  • Education: the University of Evansville, a private school founded in 1854 with about 3,050 students, and the University of Southern Indiana, a public school founded in 1965 just outside the city limits.

Chemicals make up 64% of the metro area's international exports. The Census Bureau counted about $2.85 billion in health care and social assistance receipts in the city for 2022.

The University of Evansville and the University of Southern Indiana also draw students to the area.

What is the flood risk in Evansville?

Evansville sits behind a levee system built after the 1937 Ohio River flood. The river crested at 53.7 feet on January 31, 1937, the flood covered about 500 city blocks, and the city was placed under martial law.

The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers began construction in 1939 and work was completed in 1994. According to the state historical marker, the project includes 17 miles of earth levees and concrete floodwalls and 19 pumping stations, and it protects against flood water up to 57 feet. The Evansville-Vanderburgh Levee Authority District maintains it.

  • The eastern levees closely follow I-69.
  • Pigeon Creek has been widened and leveed, and Ohio River backwater affects the whole county, according to a 2023 presentation to county commissioners.
  • That presentation notes the creek's average annual peak flow at the Fort Branch gauge rose from about 2,350 to 2,820 cubic feet per second over 35 years.

Indiana's seller disclosure asks the owner to say whether they know the property is in a FEMA flood plain. A buyer or lender may ask for flood zone and insurance details, so find out your parcel's status before you sell.

How hot, wet and snowy is Evansville?

Evansville has a humid subtropical climate with hot, humid summers and cool winters. Average temperatures run from about 32.5 degrees Fahrenheit in January to 78 in July.

Annual precipitation is about 45.3 inches, with 11.8 inches of snow. The record high is 111 degrees on July 28, 1930, and the record low is minus 23 on February 2, 1951. Humid summers and 45 inches of rain make roof condition, drainage and basement moisture standard inspection topics.

Evansville regulates rental dwellings under Chapter 15.16 of its municipal code, and the Building Commission runs a rental registry. Registration is required for substandard rental buildings and voluntary for well-kept ones.

  • Required registration fee: $100.00 per dwelling unit.
  • Voluntary registration fee: $10.00 per dwelling unit, with a signed affidavit that the building meets the property maintenance code.
  • A voluntary permit lasts one year or until title transfers, and covers up to $3,000 of maintenance work per unit.

Owners must report an ownership change within 30 days, and a prior registration expires 30 days after title transfers. Code officials may give an owner at least 10 calendar days to fix a violation, and an owner ordered to register may appeal in writing within 10 calendar days of service.

The city has moved rental registrations to an online platform. Call the Rental Registry at the Building Commission, 812-436-7887, with questions.

Property maintenance enforcement, including weeds, trash and existing structures, falls under the Building Commission. Indiana taxes are due in two installments, listed by the state as May 11 and November 10 for 2026, with a 5% penalty up to 30 days late and 10% after that.

Hamilton County also contains Carmel, Noblesville (the county seat), Westfield and several smaller towns. After the 2020 census, Fishers ranked sixth among Indiana cities and towns by population. Fishers began as a rail siding. William Conner settled the area in 1802, the Peru and Indianapolis Railroad started construction in 1849, and Salathial Fisher platted Fisher's Switch in 1872. The place was incorporated as the town of Fisher's Station in 1891, and in 1908 the post office dropped "Switch" from the name.

It became a town on December 4, 1883, and the population climbed with the mills and rail yards until it peaked at 111,698 in 1960. The 2020 census counted 77,879 residents, which makes Hammond the eighth-largest city in Indiana.

That growth pattern left a large stock of early and mid-twentieth century housing: worker cottages, bungalows and two-flats. Several neighborhoods are listed as historic districts, including Forest-Ivanhoe, Forest-Moraine, Glendale Park, Indi-Illi Park, Pullman-Standard and Roselawn-Forest Heights. Where is Hobart, Indiana?

Hobart is a city in Lake County, Indiana, about 31 miles southeast of Chicago. It covers 26.57 square miles at an elevation of 627 feet, and its ZIP code is 46342.

The city sits on Deep River, where an early dam formed Lake George. The lake sits beside the downtown and lakefront area. The city's retail corridor lies near the point where Interstate 65 meets U.S. Route 30.

Gary/Chicago International Airport, Midway and O'Hare are the nearby airports listed for the area, and a small private field, Hobart Sky Ranch Airport, is 2 miles north of downtown.

What is the history of Hobart?

Hobart was platted in 1849 and grew around a dam built on Deep River by English immigrant George Earle, who bought land from the Potawatomi. The settlement took its name from his brother, Frederick Hobart Earle, who never left England.

The first school was built in 1878. Hobart was incorporated as a town in 1889 and reincorporated as a city in 1921. Several downtown buildings are on the National Register of Historic Places, including the Hobart Carnegie Library, the Pennsylvania Railroad Station, the Hobart Commercial District and the First Unitarian Church of Hobart.

A city platted in the nineteenth century and reincorporated in 1921 has a mix of older homes and later additions, and a house's age often decides how much updating a buyer expects. Annexation also brought in the newer retail corridor.

The Census Bureau puts Hobart's median owner-occupied home value at $215,200 for 2020 to 2024, with 69.5% of homes owner-occupied. The 2020 Census counted 29,752 residents and 12,709 housing units, with 5.6% of units vacant.

What is the Hobart economy like?

Hobart has long been mostly residential, and a retail corridor was added by annexation. Southlake Mall, a super-regional mall near U.S. Route 30 and Interstate 65, anchors that area with many surrounding stores and restaurants.

Local businesses include Indiana Botanic Gardens, which moved to Hobart in the mid-1990s and is described as the nation's largest and oldest herb retailer, and Midwest Products, which has been headquartered in Hobart since 1952 and makes hobby materials and radio-controlled model aircraft. A downtown shopping district includes the historic Art Theatre.

Three railroads run through the city: Norfolk Southern, Chicago, Fort Wayne and Eastern, and Canadian National. Train noise can affect homes near the tracks, and buyers sometimes ask about it, so be ready to answer honestly.

Which school districts serve Hobart?

Most of Hobart is in the School City of Hobart. Some parts of the city fall in the River Forest Community School Corporation or the Merrillville Community School District.

Hobart High School teams are called the Brickies, and its band won national Sousa competitions under William Revelli in the early twentieth century. Private options include Trinity Lutheran School and Montessori Academy in the Oaks.

Buyers with children often check which district a street belongs to, so confirm your address on the district's boundary information before you describe it in a listing or an offer conversation.

What flood and weather risks affect Hobart homes?

Hobart has a documented flood history. The U.S. Geological Survey's report on the September 2008 flood in northwestern Indiana lists Hobart among eleven communities where flooding was especially severe.

That storm brought between 2 and more than 11 inches of rain over September 12 to 15, 2008. The flood caused two deaths and evacuations of hundreds of residents, and six northwestern Indiana counties were declared federal disaster areas.

If your Hobart house is near Deep River, Lake George or a creek, here is what to gather before selling:

  • Any flood insurance policy and claim history.
  • Repair receipts for sump pumps, drainage and basement work.
  • A FEMA flood map check for the parcel.
  • Photos of the basement after heavy rain, if you have them.

Disclosing known water problems on the Indiana seller disclosure keeps a sale clean, and cash buyers usually price the risk in rather than walk away.

Hobart's lakefront is the best-known draw. Lake George offers walking, fishing and boating, and Lakefront Park has a clock tower and the Revelli Bandshell, where music is played in warm months.

The city has 14 parks and a public 18-hole golf course. The Oak Savannah rails-to-trails route passes through and runs by the 90-acre Hobart Prairie Grove Unit of Indiana Dunes National Park, and Cressmoor Prairie is a state nature preserve and the largest state-protected black-soil prairie in Indiana.

Homes near the lake, the trails or downtown tend to be the ones buyers ask about first, so mention proximity accurately.

What city rules apply to Hobart property owners?

Hobart's Building Department issues building permits and inspects new construction and remodeling inside city limits. Permits are required before any work starts, and the department also licenses contractors and handles building-related code complaints. It is at 414 Main St., with a phone number of 219-942-1722 and an email of building@cityofhobart.org.

Hobart also requires rental registration. Under Chapter 115 of the municipal code, an owner of rental property registers each year with the Building Department by July 15. Registration requires proof of insurance, or a bond or letter of credit of at least $25,000. A property acquired after July 15 must be registered within 30 days of purchase, and a sale, transfer or end of rental use must be reported within 30 days.

Failure to register can bring a fine of up to $2,500 per unit per day, and repeat violations can reach $7,500 per unit per day. If you are selling a rented house, make sure the registration is current and tell the buyer what rules come with the property.

How does a sale close and get recorded in Lake County?

Deeds for Hobart properties are recorded with the Lake County Recorder in Crown Point, at 2293 N. Main Street, Building A, 2nd Floor. The office is open Monday through Friday from 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., and its phone is 219-755-3730.

The recorder handles deeds, mortgages, liens, releases and leases. It does not generally record court orders, decrees, judgments or wills, so an inherited house usually needs the right probate paperwork sorted out before a deed can be prepared.

Indiana requires the parties to a transfer to complete a sales disclosure form, which the county assessor reviews and the county auditor files before the conveyance document is filed. Property tax is due in two installments, May 10 and November 10. A title company usually coordinates all of this.

Where is Marion, Indiana?

Marion is the county seat of Grant County, on the Mississinewa River in north central Indiana. It covers about 15.8 square miles and sits at an elevation near 814 feet.

The 2020 census counted 28,310 residents, and the Census Bureau's 2025 estimate is 28,234. The population peaked at 39,607 in 1970, a decline of about 11,000 residents that still shapes the local market.

The ZIP codes are 46952 and 46953 and the area code is 765. The city runs on a mayor-council form of government with nine council members, six by ward and three at large.

A short history of Marion

Martin Boots and David Branson each donated 30 acres in 1831 to start the town, which was incorporated as a city in 1889 and named for Revolutionary War general Francis Marion.

The Indiana gas boom of the 1880s fed rapid growth, and nearby Gas City and Matthews boomed with it. In 1888 Congress set up the Marion Branch of the National Home for Disabled Volunteer Soldiers with a $200,000 appropriation, which became today's VA presence on the southeast side. The 212 acre Marion Branch Historic District lies about 2.5 miles southeast of downtown.

The city is linked to actor James Dean and Garfield creator Jim Davis, and it bills itself as Christmas City U.S.A., with a Walkway of Lights along nearly 4 miles of the Riverwalk.

What drives the Marion economy?

Manufacturing has been the base for generations, including automotive components, paper products, foundry goods, machinery, wire and cable. The paper plate industry began in Marion, and a General Motors stamping and tool plant opened in the 1950s.

Plant closures hit the city hard. Thomson SA closed in 2004 and TriEnda Plastics stopped production by spring 2011.

  • Indiana Wesleyan University is the largest evangelical Christian university in the Midwest and Indiana's largest private university, counting online and regional campuses. The traditional campus enrolls about 2,800 students.
  • The VA Northern Indiana Health Care System runs the Marion campus.
  • Marion General Hospital is a nationally accredited hospital with magnet status.

Sports and events add to local identity. The Marion Giants have won eight state basketball championships and play at the 7,500 seat Bill Green Athletic Arena, and the Mississinewa 1812 festival hosts what is described as the largest War of 1812 reenactment in the U.S., recalling the December 1812 battle fought about 7 miles downstream.

Agriculture surrounds the city, with corn, soybeans, hogs and tomatoes in the Corn Belt around it.

Records run from 108 degrees F in July to minus 23 degrees F in winter. That range stresses roofs, siding, furnaces and plumbing in unheated houses.

Marion Municipal Airport is about three nautical miles southwest of the central business district, and the Marion Transit System runs fixed-route and demand-response buses.

Marion requires owners of residential rental properties, rooming houses and apartment buildings to register with the Building Department. The requirement started January 1, 2020, and applications go to Marion Building / Code Enforcement at 301 S. Branson St., phone 765-662-9931, per the city's rental registration page.

The city's 2018 Neighborhood Preservation Ordinance sets minimum standards for all buildings.

  • Foundations, roofs, gutters, windows, doors, stairs and porches must be maintained.
  • Vacant buildings must be locked and secured and can be classified as unsafe.
  • Tarps on a structure are limited to 30 days, and the owner must tell the building department first.
  • Repairs are due within 30 days of a notice, or 15 days for unsafe buildings.
  • Fines run up to $500, and each day counts as a separate offense.

Owners outside Indiana must appoint a local agent within 30 miles, with a $500 civil penalty per parcel for failing to do so. If you inherited a house in Marion from afar, this applies to you.

The Building Commissioner can order a building vacated, sealed, repaired or demolished. Orders name the responsible party, the action required and a deadline, and most can be appealed to the Marion Board of Public Works and Safety, with hearings at least 10 days after notice.

Owners get 72 hours written notice before a routine inspection. Debris from a demolition cannot stay on the lot more than three months. A buyer who purchases a damaged house as-is takes over those obligations, which is often the reason a seller with a deteriorated house prefers a cash sale.

Unpaid taxes can lead to a tax sale. The county's 2026 sale is set for October 26, 2026, and the certified list held 672 properties. The minimum bid covers delinquent taxes, current-year taxes, penalties and costs. For certificates sold, the redemption period ends October 26, 2027, with redemption costing 110 percent of the minimum bid within six months and 115 percent later, plus certain added costs.

If your house is on that list, selling before the sale is one way to clear it, because a property is removed if the full judgment amount is paid first.

Wikipedia names Franklin, Needham and Pleasant among the townships around the city, and notes that Needham, Franklin and Union townships merged in January 2022.

With about 26,743 residents in the Census Bureau's 2025 estimate, Franklin is a small city next to a very large one.

What is the history behind Franklin's houses?

Franklin was platted in 1823 and named for Benjamin Franklin. Its post office opened in 1824, and the town was incorporated as a city in 1861.

Franklin College, a four-year liberal arts school founded in 1834, was the first college in Indiana to admit women. In the early 1920s the high school basketball team known as the Wonder Five won three straight state titles, from 1920 to 1922. What happened in the 2008 Franklin flood, and does it still matter?

In June 2008, Canary Creek, Hurricane Creek and related waterways overflowed, and more than 100 houses were damaged or destroyed. Some entire neighborhoods were affected.

The city and county then bought out flooded properties. An Indianapolis Business Journal report in 2013 said 107 homes would have been razed once the last six came down, using about $8.5 million in federal money. A 2014 report on one neighborhood described about 70 small homes destroyed by several feet of water, with the land since reforested by volunteers who planned 4,000 to 4,500 trees. The parks department maintains the site.

Flood maps were also contested. A 2015 report on proposed FEMA changes said many of the changes involved Canary Ditch, which runs through the north and west sides of the city, and that about 70 percent of Franklin's industrial areas fell in the 100-year flood zone under the proposal. A local insurance agent quoted in the story estimated that homeowners in newly designated areas could need flood coverage costing $1,500 or more a year.

  • Look up the parcel on FEMA's current flood map before you list, since the 2015 maps were proposals at the time of that report.
  • Ask your insurer whether the house has a flood policy and what it costs.
  • If your home was damaged in 2008 or since, gather repair records and permits.

The buyouts left open ground where houses once stood, so a street near the old flood area may now back onto trees and trails instead of neighbors. Freight rail runs through town on the Louisville and Indiana Railroad. Franklin Flying Field is about 3.5 miles south of downtown, and Indianapolis International Airport is about 28 miles northwest. Access Johnson County provides bus service.

Where is Greenfield, Indiana?

Greenfield is the county seat of Hancock County, in central Indiana, and it is part of the Indianapolis metropolitan area. Downtown Indianapolis is about 21 miles to the west along U.S. 40.

The city lies in Center and Brandywine townships and covers about 13.7 square miles. Brandywine Creek runs through Riley Park on the east side of downtown and flows south toward the Big Blue River. What is the history behind Greenfield?

Hancock County was created on March 1, 1828, and Greenfield was picked as county seat on April 11 of that year, when the county had about 400 residents. It became a city in 1876.

The National Road, now U.S. 40, came through around 1835, and the first steam railroad arrived in 1851. Natural gas was found in 1887 and set off a boom of about 20 years that brought new plants to town. A statue of poet James Whitcomb Riley, paid for by schoolchildren across the country, was put up in front of the courthouse in 1918, and the Riley Festival still fills the square each October.

The Greenfield Courthouse Square Historic District and the Greenfield Residential Historic District are both on the National Register of Historic Places. Houses in those districts are older, and older houses usually come with roofs, wiring and plaster that a buyer's inspector will look at closely.

East Chicago is a Lake County city on the shore of Lake Michigan, about 18 miles from downtown Chicago and just west of Gary. It covers about 14.9 square miles, including roughly 0.7 square miles of water.

How did steel shape East Chicago?

Steel made East Chicago. The town incorporated in 1889 and became a city in 1893. Its population was 1,255 in 1890 and 3,411 by 1900.

Inland Steel arrived in 1903, and the Indiana Harbor Ship Canal gave the mills a navigable link to Lake Michigan by 1907. Inland's capacity grew from 60,000 tons in 1903 to a peak of 8.6 million tons in 1978. During World War I the city was nicknamed the Arsenal of America.

The steel crisis of 1974 to 1986 cut into jobs, and ownership of the mills changed several times: Ispat International bought Inland Steel in 1998, the mills were merged into ArcelorMittal in 2004, and Cleveland-Cliffs bought them in 2020. Cleveland-Cliffs' Indiana Harbor Works is described as the largest steel mill in the United States.

  • Other employers named for the city: U.S. Steel's East Chicago Tin, Union Tank Car, American Steel Foundries, USG and St. Catherine Hospital.
  • A casino opened in 1997 as the Showboat Casino with about 900 employees.

Indiana Harbor was where most of the mill's working families lived, which explains why the city's older housing sits close to the industrial lakefront.

East Chicago has long been described as a twin city. Indiana Harbor, the East Side, grew around Inland Steel and housed most working families, while the West Side was the residential area of the native-born business community.

Two sites in the city are on the National Register of Historic Places: the Marktown Historic District and the Indiana Harbor Public Library. A house in Marktown may be subject to rules for historic properties, which a buyer will ask about.
